J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "Therefore there exists i, 1 <= i <= k, such that the edges {v1, vi+1} and {vi, vk} belong to E." First-choice line 11 contains that verbatim: "Therefore there exists i, $1 \le i \le k$, that $\{v_1, v_{i+1}\}$, $\{v_i, v_k\}$ $\in$ E". Line 11 is the whole proof attempt, and the assumptions it puts in force are exactly G = (V,E), P an arbitrary path on v_1..v_k ("suppose P is a path in G" -- deliberately not a longest path, as line 9 states: "I haven't assumed that P is the longest path"), and every vertex of degree at least n/2. So the line asserts the challenged existence claim under those assumptions.

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A concrete graph and a concrete path: "In K3,3 (n=6, minimum degree 3 >= n/2) take the path P = a1-b1-a2-b2-a3; no index i satisfies both required edges." The reasoning also walks the four candidate indices explicitly. Graph, degree check, path and the failing quantifier are all supplied.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exact enumeration of the supplied witness, script kept. In K_{3,3} every vertex has degree 3 and n = 6, so the source's hypothesis (degree at least n/2) holds with equality; P = a1-b1-a2-b2-a3 is a genuine path (all four consecutive pairs are edges, five distinct vertices), so it is an admissible P for line 11, which requires nothing more of P. Checking every i from 1 to k = 5: i=1 gives {v1,v2} in E but {v1,vk} = {a1,a3} not in E; i=2 gives {v1,v3} = {a1,a2} not in E; i=3 gives {v1,v4} in E but {v3,vk} = {a2,a3} not in E; i=4 gives {v1,v5} = {a1,a3} not in E; i=5 has no v_6 at all. No index satisfies both conditions, so the asserted existence fails at a point satisfying the assumptions in force -- a genuine refutation of the line as written. The script also records that the same line's earlier claim (v_1 joined to at least n/2 vertices among v_2..v_k) fails on the same witness, a1 having only b1 and b2 as neighbours on P, which is the root of the failed inference; and that K_{3,3} is itself Hamiltonian, so the defect is in the argument and not in Dirac's theorem.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The consequence the response states is exactly scoped to the step: "Without assuming P is longest, you cannot guarantee such i exists" and "This is not guaranteed under just degree >= n/2 if P is not a longest path." It states Dirac's theorem correctly at the outset ("If G is a simple graph on n >= 3 vertices with minimum degree delta(G) >= n/2, then G is Hamiltonian") and never suggests the theorem or the Hamiltonicity conclusion is false -- only that this route to it is unsupported. No overreach.

notes: For a second reader: line 11 contains several assertions and the witness invalidates the inference chain at more than one point (both the 'v_1 is connected to at least n/2 vertices from v_2 to v_k' step and the 'therefore there exists i' step fail on K_{3,3} with this path). A strict reader might say the quoted sentence fails only because an earlier sentence of the same line fails; since both sit on line 11, that does not change the verdict on the first-choice label. Note also that the response's discursive reasoning briefly floats a different and weaker objection ('the ordering they gave is not necessarily a simple cycle ... they repeat vertices maybe incorrectly'), which it does not rely on in its final claim; I graded only the final claim and witness. The source's degree hypothesis is met with equality in K_{3,3}, so a reader who insisted on strict inequality degree > n/2 would want a different witness; the source writes 'at least n/2'.
